parts.latex:
The length and width of a rectangle are measured to be 8 cm and 5 cm respectively, to the nearest centimetre.

What are the lower and upper bounds for the area of the rectangle?
parts.note: Limits of accuracy (upper and lower bounds of measurements) are not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
Each measurement is correct to the nearest centimetre, so it can be up to $0.5$ cm either side.
$$\begin{aligned} 7.5 \le \text{length} &< 8.5\\ 4.5 \le \text{width} &< 5.5\end{aligned}$$
Lower bound of the area uses the lower bounds:
$$7.5\times 4.5 = 33.75 \text{ cm}^2$$
Upper bound of the area uses the upper bounds:
$$8.5\times 5.5 = 46.75 \text{ cm}^2$$
This is option D.

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written from answer key D.

solutions.latex:
The table gives the area below $z$. For $z = 1.94$ the table value is
$$P(Z < 1.94) = 0.9738$$
The distribution is symmetric about 0, so $P(Z<0) = 0.5$.

The probability between 0 and 1.94 is the area below 1.94 less the area below 0:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0 < Z < 1.94) &= 0.9738 - 0.5 \\ &= 0.4738 \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
A plant stem is measured to be 16.0 cm, correct to one decimal place.

What is the percentage error in this measurement?
parts.note: Percentage error of a measurement is not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
A measurement correct to one decimal place has an absolute error (precision) of half the unit of measurement:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 0.1 = 0.05 \text{ cm}$$
The percentage error is the absolute error divided by the measurement:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{percentage error} &= \dfrac{0.05}{16.0}\times 100\% \\ &= 0.3125\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the percentage error is } 0.3125\%$$

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written from the answer key (A).

parts.latex:
The capacity of a bottle is measured as 1.35 litres correct to the nearest 10 millilitres.

What is the absolute error as a percentage for this measurement, to two decimal places?
parts.note: Percentage error of a measurement is measurement error, not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
The measurement is correct to the nearest $10 \text{ mL}$, so the absolute error is half of this.
$$\text{Absolute error} = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5 \text{ mL}$$
Convert the measurement to millilitres: $1.35 \text{ L} = 1350 \text{ mL}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error} &= \dfrac{5}{1350}\times 100\% \\ &\approx 0.37\% \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is B.

parts.latex:
Rowan measured the length of a wall to be 3.6 metres.

Calculate the percentage error in this measurement, correct to three significant figures.
parts.note: Percentage error in measurement is not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
The absolute error is half the smallest unit, $0.05$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error} &= \dfrac{0.05}{3.6} \times 100\% \\ &\approx 1.39\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 1.39\%$$

parts.latex: Using the table, show that the probability that a value from a random variable that is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 is greater than 0.3 is equal to 0.3821.

parts.latex: Birth weights are normally distributed with a mean of 3300 grams and a standard deviation of 570 grams. By first calculating a $z$-score, find how many babies, out of 1000 born, are expected to have a birth weight greater than 3471 grams.
parts.note: Normal probability from a z-table after calculating a z-score; z-table probabilities are not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
By symmetry, $P(Z>0)=0.5$, and the table gives $P(0<Z<0.3)=0.1179$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z>0.3) &= 0.5 - 0.1179 \\ &= 0.3821 \end{aligned}$$

The $z$-score is
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{3471 - 3300}{570} \\ &= 0.3 \end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $P(Z > 0.3) = 0.3821$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Expected number} &= 1000\times 0.3821 \\ &= 382.1 \end{aligned}$$
About 382 babies are expected to have a birth weight greater than 3471 grams.
criteria: Calculates the $z$-score and uses the associated probability, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A person’s weight is measured as 79.3 kg.

What is the absolute error of this measurement?
parts.note: Absolute error of a measurement is not in the 2024 course

solutions.latex:
The absolute error is half of the smallest unit of measurement.

The weight is given to the nearest $0.1 \text{ kg}$, which is $100$ grams.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Absolute error} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100 \\ &= 50 \text{ grams} \end{aligned}$$

Hence the answer is $50$ grams, option B.

meta.self_check: Absolute error is half the precision unit: 0.1 kg = 100 g, so 50 g.

Cumulative percentage after 'Train or bus delay' is $92\%$, and after 'Appointment' it is $86\%$.

$$92\% - 86\% = 6\%$$

Check: the bars are $190, 142, 97, 30, 24, 16$, a total of $499$, and $30$ is about $6\%$ of $499$.

Hence the answer is $6\%$, option A.

parts.latex:
Amanda uses 80 kilocalories of energy per kilometre while she is running.

She eats a burger that contains 2180 kilojoules of energy. How many kilometres will she need to run to use up all the energy from the burger? Give your answer correct to one decimal place. (1 kilocalorie = 4.184 kilojoules)
parts.note: Food energy in kilocalories and kilojoules is not in the 2024 course

solutions.latex:
Convert kilojoules to kilocalories.
$$\begin{aligned} 2180 \text{ kilojoules} &= \dfrac{2180}{4.184} \\ &= 521.03 \text{ kilocalories} \end{aligned}$$
Distance to run:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{521.03}{80} &= 6.5129\ldots \\ &\approx 6.5 \text{ km (one decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides one correct conversion of energy, or equivalent merit
